posts.title: Indigo for the cold months
posts.excerpt: The first cool week of autumn is when we pour the winter patterns. A note on the first batch.
posts.content:
The first cool week of autumn is when we pour the winter patterns. A note on the first batch.

Cold water, deeper blue

Indigo takes more slowly in cold water, and the blue it leaves is deeper and calmer.

Sayo waits for the river to cool before she pours the plum blossoms.

Thirty cloths, two pours

The first batch was the Ume Blossoms, folded on Tuesday morning and poured twice by noon.

By Thursday they were hanging under the skylight, a little paler than last year, which is how she likes them.

The river tells you when the season has turned.

Sayo Kurata

posts.title: Cutting a stencil
posts.excerpt: Every pattern begins as a sheet of persimmon-tanned paper and a very small knife. Ren explains how.
posts.content:
Every pattern begins as a sheet of persimmon-tanned paper and a very small knife. Ren explains how.

The paper

Two layers of washi glued with persimmon tannin and smoked for a week, so the paper stays flat in wet paste.

A good sheet lasts about two hundred cloths.

The cut

Ren cuts toward himself with a short knife, turning the paper rather than the blade.

The fine bridges that hold the pattern together are the hardest part, and the first to tear.

The stencil remembers every slip of the knife.

Ren Ogino

posts.title: A cloth with ten uses
posts.excerpt: Towel, wrap, scarf, wall hanging: a short list of the ways our customers use a tenugui.
posts.content:
Towel, wrap, scarf, wall hanging: a short list of the ways our customers use a tenugui.

In the kitchen

A tenugui dries a bowl without leaving lint, and it is dry again before the next one.

Folded in four, it is also a good pot holder.

Away from home

Wrap a lunch box or a bottle, use it as a hand towel at the bath, or tie it around your neck on a hot day.

The best cloth is the one you reach for without thinking.

Hana Ide

posts.title: Why the ends are cut
posts.excerpt: People often ask why our tenugui are not hemmed at the short ends. The answer is the drying.
posts.content:
People often ask why our tenugui are not hemmed at the short ends. The answer is the drying.

Dry in an hour

A hem holds water. Without one, a tenugui dries in about an hour in the shade, even in the wet season.

A little fraying

The ends fray a few threads in the first washes and then stop. Trim them with scissors and the cloth looks new again.

A tenugui should always be dry by the time you need it.

Hana Ide

posts.title: The river rinse
posts.excerpt: Behind the workshop a channel of river water runs through a stone basin. It is where every cloth is rinsed.
posts.content:
Behind the workshop a channel of river water runs through a stone basin. It is where every cloth is rinsed.

Running water

The rice paste comes away only in running water, so the town’s dye workshops were all built by the river.

Ours draws water through a channel dug in the 1960s.

Clear water

We use dyes that fix in the cloth and leave the rinse nearly clear, and the basin is cleaned every week.

The river does half of the work.

Sayo Kurata

posts.title: The plum stencil
posts.excerpt: The plum blossom stencil was cut by Sayo’s grandfather and is still poured every winter.
posts.content:
The plum blossom stencil was cut by Sayo’s grandfather and is still poured every winter.

An old sheet

The stencil has been backed with silk mesh twice, so it has outlived every other sheet in the drawer.

Copying it

Ren traced it this summer to cut a new one. The blossoms on the copy are a little rounder; we will keep both.

An old stencil is a letter from the person who cut it.

Ren Ogino

productCategories.name: Patterned
productCategories.description: Stencil and freehand patterns, pour-dyed through thirty layers.

products.name: Seigaiha Waves
products.short: Overlapping waves in two indigos, the oldest pattern in our stencil drawer and still the one we pour most.
products.description:
Overlapping waves in two indigos, the oldest pattern in our stencil drawer and still the one we pour most.

Each wave is cut by hand into persimmon-tanned paper, then the stencil is laid on the cloth twenty-four times along its length. Two indigos are poured through the stack, so the waves sit slightly apart from their shadows.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Asanoha Hemp Leaf
products.short: The six-pointed hemp-leaf star in a fine dyer’s blue, a pattern given to new babies for a long and straight life.
products.description:
The six-pointed hemp-leaf star in a fine dyer’s blue, a pattern given to new babies for a long and straight life.

Hemp grows fast and straight, so the asanoha was the cloth of first kimonos. Our stencil is cut finer than most: from a step away the star turns into a soft blue texture.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Mameshibori Dots
products.short: Small pale dots on a deep indigo ground, the plainest pattern we make and the one people buy twice.
products.description:
Small pale dots on a deep indigo ground, the plainest pattern we make and the one people buy twice.

Mameshibori means bean dots. The ground is poured dark and the dots are kept pale by a paste of rice and bran, washed away in the river rinse. Every dot is a little different.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Shima Stripes
products.short: Uneven stripes in three blues, poured without a stencil so no two cloths line up the same.
products.description:
Uneven stripes in three blues, poured without a stencil so no two cloths line up the same.

The stripes are poured freehand along the length of the folded stack, one blue at a time. The narrowest are barely a finger wide; the widest fall where the kettle lingers.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Ume Blossoms
products.short: Small plum blossoms scattered on off-white, poured each year from the first cold week until the blossoms open.
products.description:
Small plum blossoms scattered on off-white, poured each year from the first cold week until the blossoms open.

Plum flowers before any other tree, often in snow, so the pattern is a quiet wish for the year ahead. We pour it only in winter and stop when the trees by the river bloom.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Ame Rain
products.short: Fine slanted lines of rain in pale and deep indigo, our pattern for the wet weeks of early summer.
products.description:
Fine slanted lines of rain in pale and deep indigo, our pattern for the wet weeks of early summer.

The rain stencil has more than four hundred cuts and takes Ren three days. The lines are poured in two indigos, so the rain seems to fall in front of itself.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Bokashi Gradient
products.short: One long fade from off-white to deep indigo, poured slowly from one end of the stack to the other.
products.description:
One long fade from off-white to deep indigo, poured slowly from one end of the stack to the other.

Bokashi is the hardest pour we make: the dye is thinned a little with every pass, so the colour fades without a line. Two cloths in a batch of thirty usually come out just right.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.

products.name: Three-cloth Gift Set
products.short: Three cloths of your choice, folded and tied with undyed cotton cord, with a card on how to use them.
products.description:
Three cloths of your choice, folded and tied with undyed cotton cord, with a card on how to use them.

Choose three patterns in the note at checkout, or leave it to us and we will pick three that sit well together. The set is wrapped in plain paper, without plastic.

Every cloth is poured by hand, so the pattern and the depth of blue vary slightly from the photograph. Wash it once on its own before the first use; see How to use & care.
